I should like to ask the sponsor of the bill one or two questions. I am concerned with the ramifications of the bill only from one or two angles. It is proposed under this merger that the Ontario and Minnesota Power company shall absorb four or five other companies. The reasons given are that it is more economical to have one administration take care of the whole organization, instead of having five do so. I 14873-2111
am concerned about the lives of the people employed in the companies which are being taken over.
We have had a great deal of experience in Canada with mergers of this kind. We know that smaller companies may be operating in small communities. Certain wage rates apply. Local management is in control. When the merger goes through, power is vested in the parent company, and local management no longer has jurisdiction. Wage rates are subject to fixation by the parent company. Concentration of production automatically follows. Certain smaller companies must fold up-we hear that that is good economics. As a result, we find that sometimes whole communities are wiped out.
This has happened, and it can be repeated in a set-up similar to this one. I should like assurance from the sponsor of the bill that the wage rates in effect in smaller companies will remain, that local management will continue to have the same jurisdiction, and that under this set-up there is no danger of forming a monopoly which would concentrate production in one company and wipe out communities which had been engaged in similar operations.

maintopic: ONTARIO AND MINNESOTA POWER COMPANY LIMITED
speechtext: The two towns directly affected by the bill are Fort Frances and Kenora. The mayors of both of these towns have telegraphed me approving this procedure. The province of Ontario has also agreed that it is a proper thing to do. The wage rates in the paper mills operating in these two towns are, I believe, the highest in Canada. There is not a chance in the world, so far as it is possible to see, for anything the hon. member has visualized taking place. The management makes its agreements with the various mills, and it has done so right along. I know of no reason why it should change. So far as I can see, or so far as anybody else can see at the present time, there is no possible chance of any of these communities being adversely affected by what is about to take place.

I am opposed to the granting of what I consider to be the natural resources of the country, and handing them over without fee or payment to a company to develop, to be sold back to the people for whatever they can get. In my opinion, the natural resources of a country are the birthright of the people, I do not care whether they are mines, water power, forests, asbestos deposits, the Alberta oil fields or lumber. All these natural resources belong to the people, and when they are handed over to a company in this way the people get practically nothing

On section 13-Interpretation.

When we took recess at the dinner hour I was making some observations with respect to the tax on amusements. I think I had proceeded to the point where I had endeavoured to convince the minister that a tax of 20 per cent on the gross takings of the small picture houses would constitute a very onerous burden indeed and, having regard to the other imposts on such small enterprises, would, in my view, perhaps drive them out of business. I am convinced of the truth of the observations which I have made. I do not think I should labour the point any further.
When the announcement was made in the budget speech that this form of amusement or entertainment was singled out for taxation, even as a war measure, it produced a strong protest in the country, not only from the proprietors and those immediately interested, but from the patrons of the business as well. The minister was well advised to change the base of the tax, although it is not usual for a Minister of Finance to do so. In peace time the proprietors of this class of business would have protested vigorously against the tax; but because we are at war and the money is needed, they have decided, as good citizens of Canada, to acquiesce in the principle of the tax provided that other commercial amusements are treated in the same way; and I believe the minister did well to adopt that point of view.
That, of course, opens up a very large field. I assume that the minister has received a number of protests with respect to commercialized sport-if I may properly use that term. If motion pictures are to be taxed, so should commercialized sport also. I see no
reason why amusements such as professional hockey and professional baseball should be exempted if the common people of this country are to be taxed on such amusements as motion, pictures. When I visualize one of my friends and fellow citizens travelling from Fredericton to Toronto to see a hockey match at the Maple Leaf gardens, I conclude that it must be a great spectacle and that the patrons of that form of amusement can well pay a tax, especially if, as I understand is the situation, the proprietors have the option of absorbing the tax or of passing it on to their patrons.
There is, however, a clear line of demarcation between commercialized sport and amateur sport as such; and unless the minister is of opinion that the exempt'ons contained in section 122, subsection 2 are sufficiently wide to cover the cases I 'have in mind, I believe that this tax is not well imposed. I believe that the draftsmen of this section had in mind what I also have in mind, that ordinary amateur athletic contests, when not operated for the benefit by way of personal gain of any private person or proprietor, should' not be taxed; and I am wondering whether the reservation contained in the subsection on page 9 of the bill is sufficiently wide to cover everything I had in mind.
The most pronouncedly amateur contest in the world cannot be run without money. In ordinary times, at all events in small communities, one will always find public-spirited men who put their hands in their pockets to support contests of this kind. But this is war time, and people's generous impulses to give money are diverted to the support of war-time activities, as, of course, it is proper they should be. While this is in a degree a war measure, we have no undertaking from the minister that this tax will not continue for ever. If it proves very profitable it will probably remain for, at least, a considerable time. I am not going to suggest or propose an amendment; but I hope that, in the administration of the measure, under the discretionary powers conferred upon the minister, the commissioner or whoever exercises these powers will look with great favour on anything which will help to conserve amateur athletics and all that is implied in that term.
One of the reasons why England has not been decadent in this war, as some predicted she would be, is that the Englishman still plays games, and while he is, of course, a follower of professional sport, the amateur instinct is well to the fore. Waterloo, it is said, was won on the playing fields of Eton. Well, this war may be won as the result of the athletic activities of the people of
Special War Revenue Act

England. I trust that the minister and those who are charged with the responsibility of administering this measure will exercise with great leniency their discretion in connection with amateur sports such as those to which I have referred. There may be occasions where money must be paid from the proceeds of these amateur fixtures to, we shall say, someone who owns the athletic field or the rink. This point was touched upon by the hon. member for Saskatoon City. My view is that the minister in exercising his discretion, ought to take into account such conditions as were stated here by that hon. member. You cannot have these facilities unless somebody provides them, and not many municipalities as such will provide expensive places for amateur sport. This is usually done by athletic associations, such as the one with which the minister is no doubt familiar, the Halifax Wanderers' grounds. The Wanderers Athletic association has been in existence for more than half a century. Some communities do not have these facilities, and I would ask on behalf of the youth of the country, that no tax be imposed on enterprises which are primarily amateur and for the benefit of the rising Canadian generation.

I concur in all that was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Saskatoon City, not only with regard to amateur hockey but with regard to amateur sports of all kinds. As the previous speaker pointed out, the well-being and health of the nation depend upon the development that comes from such sports, and therefore amateur sports should be fostered and developed among the younger people. I trust the minister will be able to exempt such sports. I do not see any particular harm in taxing professional sport. It is a commercial enterprise with many people, and they should make their contribution at this time. But it is most essential to the future welfare of the nation that we should at some cost develop amateur sport in Canada.
Let me also mention the moving pictures. As I have already pointed out, in Manitoba it will cost the people, in the majority of cases, an added 40 per cent on the admission fee, if we take the provincial tax into account. These people have not benefited by war industries and I submit that they should be given some consideration, even if they were taxed ten per cent. I do not see why horse racing, which is not essential at this time, should pay a tax of only 5 per cent, while these other people are asked to pay 20 per cent. It must also be remembered that sports of all kinds are essential not only from
CMr. R. B. Hanson.]
a recreational but from an educational point of view. I hope the minister will consider these two points.

Like others who have spoken, I have received telegrams from theatre owners protesting against the amusement tax. They pointed out, however, that they were not averse to the tax provided other forms oi amusement were treated similarly. In taxing everything in the way of amusement, I think the minister has offset the contention of the theatre managers.
I look at these taxes in this way. Money must be raised if we are to go through with the job in which we are engaged, of prosecuting the war; and when we compare any of these taxes with the income tax imposed on low-income groups, those receiving as little as S660 a year, and the national defence tax-and remember that the sports are purely voluntary, things that we can do without-I suggest that this is the wrong time to quibble about such matters if we are serious in our prosecution of the war and in our effort to make some sacrifices. That is how I look at the amusement tax. I know it will hit the low income groups, the theatre tax particularly. It will hit them hard. But it will not hit them nearly so hard as if the people on the other side of the water who are trying to impose upon us their way of life succeeded. As I said a few nights, ago, the minister finds himself in the position of having to conform to certain rules with regard to the raising of money, and this is the way the rules compel him to raise this money.
What I am more concerned about is the point raised by the hon. member for Saskatoon City, not as regards the promotion of amateur sport alone, because in my opinion this is the wrong time to talk about these things; there are other matters that are more serious. The hon. member, however, did point out that in certain communities-and this applies across the country-people have organized community projects such as rinks. In my own section there are two large rinks which were erected a couple of years ago. For one of these the necessary funds were raised among the miners. They subscribed ten dollars a share, and there is no profit in it for them; they expect nothing. They sponsored the project in order to have a community enterprise whereby people could be gathered together and they could promote sports of all kinds, build up the younger generation and keep them off the road. That was the main object. As regards the promotion of amateur sports, I am not so sure that it is altogether amateur, but they do run hockey games and

Special War Revenue Act
so forth, and they depend upon the income from that source to liquidate the cost of buildings. No one expects any return from the undertaking. The proviso on page 9 of the bill reads:
Provided that the minister may, in his discretion, exempt any person from payment of the tax where the sole or chief purpose of the performance ... is in his opinion charitable.
The minister in that proviso has certain discretionary powers, and after the bill is passed, the matter mentioned by the hon. member for Saskatoon City-these community rinks that are absolutely community undertakings from which there are no profits to shareholders- can be dealt with as the minister sees fit. He has the power to exempt these people from taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The proviso pretty well
speaks for itself. Something will depend upon administration, but perhaps I should say it is the intention that a fairly liberal interpretation shall be given exemptions. There are two parts to the exemption section. One is the part that does hot depend upon the discretion of the minister but exempts outright certain amusements, and the second part is that which authorizes the minister in his discretion to exempt others.
Only charitable ones.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If in his discretion the performance, exhibition or contest is charitable rather than one of gain or profit to the person or persons organizing, promoting managing or sponsoring the same. "Charitable" has a rather wide meaning in English law, and there is considerable discretion in the minister.

The minister's discretion under this section really extends only to the interpretation of the word "charitable". Like the hon. member for Davenport, I am having volume 1 of my telegrams bound, and I started on volume 2 this afternoon, although of course we cannot pay attention to all of them.
I am not entirely in agreement with the suggestion that consideration should be given only to amateur sport. Look at the history of the Maple Leaf gardens, the Maple Leaf hockey team and the Maple Leaf baseball team. When the new Maple Leaf garden was to be constructed I was one of those asked to subscribe to the stock of the company. It was not suggested that I should do so in order to make a profit; the idea was that I should help in this effort which it was thought would be beneficial to sport throughout the country. All the prominent men who have stock in that company are now to be left holding the bag. They have never made any
money out of the business; they have been motivated more by the idea of helping sport than by the idea of making money. It would be silly to put money into a proposition like that on any other basis.
There is one other point to be mentioned in connection with the Maple Leaf hockey team, and I imagine the same thing applies to the Montreal team. These are the people who are supporting amateur hockey to a very large extent. If it were not for these professional teams we would not have the class of amateur hockey that we see all over the country. I quite agree with the minister that we must get the money somehow; but as I suggested before the dinner recess, if we impose a tax as high as 20 per cent we are going to run into the law of diminishing returns. On the other hand, in a city like Toronto, if these concerns make more money, the government will be able to take more money from them under the excess profits tax. I do not think a tax of 10 per cent would make very much difference so far as professional hockey is concerned, but 20 per cent is altogether too much. We certainly should not take a chance on putting out of business the Maple Leaf hockey team or the Canadiens of Montreal, and I will tell the committee why. Teams like these are perhaps the best good-will ambassadors we have. They go to the United States and mix with the people there; there is keen rivalry between Canadian and United States teams, and that does a great deal to keep the two countries together. In addition, a great many people come here from the United States to see our hockey games, which brings more foreign exchange into the country, and it must be remembered that these two professional teams have developed many of the players on the other teams in the league. Therefore, I believe that a 20 per cent tax on all tickets will be so severe that it may defeat the very purpose the government has in mind, and it may interfere definitely with the game itself.
I do not think we wish to interfere with amateur sport, but before we discuss this at greater length I think the Minister of National Revenue should tell us just what this may mean as it will affect these various clubs. Just who will be taxed and who will not be taxed? What are the ramifications of the whole thing? Subsection 2 does not tell us very much, and I think it should be clarified. It has been said that there should be some difference between the tax on admissions to large theatres, and that on admissions to small theatres. As I pointed out before the dinner recess, already there has been a falling off in the attendance at the large theatres in my own riding. Therefore I suggest that if
Special War Revenue Act

the tax were reduced to perhaps 10 per cent the government would benefit in two ways. In the first place they would collect more under the excess profits tax, and in the second place the theatres would be filled and the revenue under this tax would not suffer. Do not empty the theatres; fill them up. Let the theatres make their profits; impose a reasonable tax on each admission, and then apply the excess profits tax to the theatres. To me that seems the logical thing to do.

Perhaps, when the minister is replying to the hon. member for St. Paul's, he will give a specific reply to the telegram I had a page take to him across the floor some two or three days ago.
While I am on my feet I should like to suggest that in many instances a tax of 20 per cent on the gross is liable to close up the industry almost entirely. No doubt the minister has given thought to the possibility of taxing the net, and perhaps he might say a word about that. Then I would direct his attention to the fact that this tax may work a hardship as between different classes of amusements. In the case of a theatrical performance the costs are far greater than in the case of a hockey match, let us say. From that I draw the conclusion that in the one case the net return in relation to the gross would not be in anything like the same proportion as in the other. The general idea is that we want to get some of the revenue which the owners and producers of these amusements are receiving, but in doing so we must not discriminate against that amusement which finds that its net is in nothing like the same proportion to its gross as is the situation with another enterprise.
I hope I have made my point clear to the minister. To follow that thought a little further, this will work a hardship on many people and will probably put some of them out of business. As the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox said this afternoon, the government may kill the goose that laid the golden egg. I am satisfied that these organizations would feel disposed to operate their amusements and turn over 100 per cent of their profits for the duration of the war, rather than lose the investments that they have at the present time, through finding it necessary to shut down. I have in mind the small community in which a moving-picture theatre is operated. It may be that theatre finds that it is just able to balance its budget, and perhaps give the proprietor a fair living. He takes his gross of $400 a week, and finds that he is subject to a tax of $80. He adds that tax to the cost of the ticket, and finds that his returns are diminishing. I believe it 
has been found in Campbellford that since this tax was instituted the numbers of those attending moving-picture theatres have dropped by one-half. I am sure there are many places where the theatres will have to close up.
If there were some way of taxing the entire profits of not only the moving-picture theatres but also of skating-rinks and other enterprises of that kind for the duration of the war, I believe it would be found that the people operating those enterprises would be sporting enough and interested enough in our cause to give over all their profits, if they were permitted to operate in a way which would permit them to balance their budgets. I should like to see some discretionary power in this measure whereby the minister could permit a skating-rink, an athletic field or a theatre in a small community to carry on, they in turn agreeing to turn over their profits for the duration of the war. In that way the industry would be kept alive; pur people would be following their usual pursuits and resuming their usual small measure of amusement and small measure of athletic interest to which they have been accustomed in the past.
We must have money. I admit at once it would be very difficult to administer a taxation system on net income. I quite appreciate it is very simple when it is done on the gross. It will, however, work hardship in certain places, and the minister should have even more discretionary powers and, as the hon. member for Rosedale has said, take a charitable view of charitable enterprises, and a charitable reading of the measure when he comes to a decision as to what is or is not a charitable organization.

I find that subsection 2 contains these words:
... no part of the revenue of which inures to the benefit or private gain of any person as proprietor or member thereof or shareholder therein-
And so forth. There are many organizations which I believe would qualify under the first part of subsection 2, but because of the nature of their corporate organizations, and because of the legal form they take, they would not qualify under the latter part of the subsection.
I have in mind the ordinary club which has no hope of making a profit for its members. Nevertheless, in order to qualify, the members may have to buy a share, and thereby they become shareholders. Therefore I should like to know if, because of the nature of that holding, and the legal possibility of a profit-

Special War Revenue Act
of course actually no such thing is contemplated-such a club is excluded from subsection 2, and must rely on the following proviso under which the minister must give consent.

It is difficult to give a ruling without having a specific case in mind. I may, however, assure the hon. member that a sympathetic view will be taken of cases such as that. We are not endeavouring to enforce taxation against organizations, societies and clubs which are obviously carrying on for the purposes set out in this section.

Possibly I might give a concrete example. The Toronto skating club and the Minto skating club hold carnivals annually. They pay out substantial sums for star performers, but the majority of the talent is contributed voluntarily. I would assume that such organizations would not be taxable.
I would not tie myself down to a ruling offhand, without having all the particulars before me. I could not possibly do that.

I tried to place the particulars before the minister, without going into great detail. Certainly, as the minister knows, no one would make a profit out of the operations of those clubs.
Another example would be that of the Argonaut rowing club. During the football season a football team operates under the name of that club, and admission prices are charged. The profits from the football games go to pay expenses for the rowing season. That sport is, I believe, fairly expensive, and not self-supporting. I take it that the members of the club are all shareholders, but I have never heard of a dividend being paid. I believe those are the cogent facts of the case, and I suggest that the minister should be able to let us know whether or not this section would cover a case like that. If not, must permission always be obtained from the minister before a game is held, or before people aTe permitted to enter without paying a tax? In respect of the Argonaut club one could hardly say that it is operated for charity, because it is operated for the benefit of the members of the club, and for the general advancement of amateur sports.

Almost every sporting organization in Toronto has been mentioned. We have heard mention of the Maple Leaf hockey team, the Toronto skating club, the Toronto baseball club, the Argonaut football club, and so on. I could not possibly give a decision offhand on the floor of the house as to whether they will be taxable or exempt, without inquiring into the set-up of each of those
organizations, and without finding out whether they comply with the provisions of the legislation. If they do, they will be exempt.

Perhaps the minister will revert to the original position that it may have been unwise to have included them under the tax. That brings me to a further point. I have no doubt that when the moving-picture industry pointed out that it was being singled out for a 20 per cent tax, while the other forms of entertainment were being left scot-free, there was the hope in their minds that the heavy imposition of a 20 per cent tax would be reduced to something more reasonable. Certainly, while misery does love company, I do not think that was the attitude of the moving-picture industry.
Perhaps I might impress upon the minister the fact that we have heard in the committee to-day, and particularly from the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox, that certain moving-picture houses in small towns have been finding that their patronage has been reduced to half. I might point out that while in the larger cities the incomes of people generally, and particularly the working class, have increased, as a result of war expenditures, and while they can absorb the 20 per cent tax, nevertheless the tax is a substantial one. The other night I went to the Capitol theatre here in Ottawa, and on two 40-cent tickets I paid sixteen cents. That is a heavy tax. I believe the minister will bear with me that in the ordinary course of business, had it been possible to advance the prices of moving-picture tickets to the extent of 20 per cent, and get away with it, without losing patronage, the proprietors would probably have done so long ago, before the tax came into force.
I think the minister must realize that he cannot boost by 20 per cent the prices of an industry like the moving-picture industry, and think it will just go on in the same way. Certainly businessmen and farmers, if I have heard correctly in this chamber, want to obtain as high prices as the traffic will bear for their products. The same applies to the proprietors of the small moving-picture theatres. They have been charging about as much as the traffic will bear. If a 20 per cent tax is imposed, it will then be found that there is a good deal in what has been said this afternoon and evening about the patronage dropping off. In that event, as the hon. member for Dan-forth stated a moment ago, you kill the goose that lays the golden eggs and create a certain amount of distress among those who operate theatres, particularly in the smaller communities. The minister did not expect to levy a tax upon amusements other than motion

Special War Revenue Act
pictures. Now that he has included these other amusements, his budget is thrown out of gear, although on the right side, and perhaps he will consider reducing this tax. If at the end of the year it is found that the people are accustomed to paying it; if the increase in the national income has made everybody a little more prosperous, then the tax could be increased to 20 per cent. Any business which must raise the price of its product 20 per cent at one fell swoop is likely to face a disastrous condition.

The only discretion the minister has is in deciding whether an amusement is being held for charitable purposes. Take the case of a boy who belongs to an amateur hockey league; under the rules he may be paid. But when the club plays a game and a gate is being collected, of necessity that club must pay this tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. member want every hockey organization that charges an admission exempted? Hon. gentlemen have been talking about exempting this and that sport. I think it was only a week ago when the unanimous sentiment of hon. members on the other side was to tax all other amusements.
Commercial amusements.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) referred to the fact that motion pictures were the poor man's amusement; that we should tax these large hockey games which attracted the big attendances. Hon. members were deluged with telegrams urging that while no exception was taken to the tax, pressure should be exerted to have the tax extended to other forms of amusement.
Commercial amusements, for gain.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have the telegrams here;
it was "other forms of amusement." If the views expressed by the hon. member for St. Paul's are accepted, as well as those expressed by other hon. members, there would be hardly any tax imposed. I have been listening for some hint as to what sport it would be proper to tax.
Commercial amusements.

I do not object
to the taxing of professional hockey. I stated that it would cut down the attendance, and I was trying to show the minister the advisability of keeping up the attendance by lowering the tax and obtaining the revenue by way of the excess profits tax. I was pointing

out that if one boy on the team was paid anything, I suppose even if he were given an outfit, it would be necessary to tax the gate. Then there is the legitimate theatre which should receive some consideration. I think there is only one theatre of this kind in Toronto and they are having a hard time. In my opinion they should be exempted. Then there is the Hart House in Toronto, the Little Theatre here in Ottawa and one theatre in Montreal. Those are about all the legitimate theatres in the country. I know the problem is difficult, but I am objecting to the minister having discretion only with respect to charitable organizations. The section has not been made clear enough. If the minister can be given discretion in these matters, I would be ready to accept his decision. I am peculiar that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A draft bill was submitted to me which gave the minister unlimited powers of exemption, and I would not sponsor it. I knew what I would get from the opposition if I brought in a bill giving the minister unlimited powers of exemption.
The minister said it could be given a wide interpretation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say that.
Would he go as far as to say that it would include the promotion of amateur athletics?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not going to attempt to distinguish as between amateur and professional, because I am advised that there is no possibility of arriving at a line of demarcation. The hon. member for St. Paul's has been talking about paid amateurs and distinguishing them from professionals.
Is the purpose of this bill to raise money or to prevent people from spending money upon what might be regarded as luxuries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would say that the first object is to raise money. But there is a secondary object. If the money is not spent for this purpose it will prove advantageous in that it will not encourage people to build theatres. Something over sixty applications have been made for permits to build new moving-picture theatres. Plans were being completed to build a chain of theatres across Canada. I thought it would be most undesirable for this country to go on a theatrebuilding spree at the very crux of a most serious war. For that reason, among others, power was taken to prevent the building of these theatres. This throws the rapidly increasing theatre business into the hands of

Special War Revenue Act
the existing theatres. These theatres sent in many telegrams protesting against permission being given to build new theatres.
I think it is commonly known to many of us that theatres in a great many parts of Canada are being crowded. Last Saturday I passed one theatre in the afternoon and another one in the evening, and in both instances a long queue of people were standing on the sidewalk waiting to buy tickets. They were all paying the tax. I do not know about the afternoon admission price, but in the case of the evening admission price they were paying a five cent tax; the price was thirty cents instead of twenty-five cents. I thought it was quite a proper tax to impose under those conditions. It places some brake on the expansion of the theatre industry; there is no doubt about that, although I would hope it would not be a serious brake. It is a heavy tax and one which, in some instances, will be harsh perhaps in its effects, but this is not the only case in which our taxation measures and our other measures have been harsh. I think of some of the things which have been done under the War Exchange Conservation Act, a measure which received wide commendation from the public and still does. But many importers, if not put completely out of business, have been very nearly put out of business. We cannot run the country having in mind only the prosperity and material well-being of everybody in the country. That is not the first consideration. It is away down in the list of considerations. Therefore this heavy tax was imposed.

But the fewer you hurt, the better. The object is not to put 'businesses out of commission because the war is on. You should not allow a business to go out of business, if it is not detracting from the war effort, if you can possibly save it. The minister must not take such a sadistic attitude toward some of these things.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What was the word?
Sadistic.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, that adjective was used in a newspaper reference to me on one occasion, and I was very much amused by it. There is nothing sadistic about my attitude.
You came close to it a minute ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at all. I wish my hon. friend would give me suggestions how to raise money instead of continually pleading the case of special taxpayers against the case of the general taxpayers of the country.

That is quite unfair. I gave the minister suggestions in my budget address. I suggested a measure of taxation which was fundamentally sound and which I thought might well be given consideration as an alternative method of raising money. Certainly the proposal which is now before the committee, with the exception of the movie end of it, is one which virtually came from this side of the house. There is no reason, as the leader of the opposition said a minute ago, why the movie industry should be singled out for taxation. The suggestion I made was that from the evidence we have had from the little centres, the movie industry has been seriously crippled. It is true that the attendance may not remain at 50 per cent of the attendance before this tax; it may go back to 75 per cent. Nevertheless it is a serious falling-off, and if a 10 per cent tax would not cripple the business too much I suggest that, if that rate of tax were imposed, then next year when the people have become more accustomed to the higher price, the tax could be raised to 20 per cent. All I am interested in is in not killing the goose that lays the golden eggs.

I do not wish to prolong this discussion; in fact, I should like to see it shortened if at all possible. 1 was looking through Hansard, which is always an interesting document, and I saw that we have already taken longer in discussing this sports and theatre tax than we took in discussing that very important tax, the national defence tax, which strikes hardest at the great masses of the lower paid workers in this country.
The hon. member has not heard us on the bill yet. That was only on the resolution. [DOT]

We have taken a greater time on this than we took on the resolution for the national defence tax, which bears so hardly on the poorer paid people of this country.
There are some things I do not like about this tax on sports. I do not like the idea of taxing amateur sport at all, but most of us realize that we must accept some taxation which we do not like. In this particular instance it seems to me that if the minister uses the discretionary power which is already in the measure and gives the word "charitable" the interpretation of which it is capable, in all probability many of the objections that have been raised can be met. I have been interested in sport all my life. I have trained many youngsters in football and other sports, and I am of opinion that we should get back to really amateur sport.

Hear, hear.
Special War Revenue Act

I have no sympathy with the team that puts a player on and pays him, and still calls itself amateur. I believe that practice is undermining our Canadian sports, and consequently I would not make any special plea for those who are doing it.
I did not quite like this tax when it was confined to movie theatres because, after all, that is the poor man's pleasure in many instances, and I think the extension of the tax, although it may work a hardship in cases such as that mentioned by the hon. member for Saskatoon City this afternoon, makes it much better than it was originally. I should like to see the committee adopt this measure because I am quite sure of this. Judging from the minister's stubbornness-
Oh, no.

-in connection with the gasoline tax, in which I was very much interested, and the national defence tax, in which I was greatly interested, we can talk to him all night on this tax, and we shall end up in exactly the same position we are in now.

Is that a sadistic attitude? I should like to give the Minister of Finance what a friend of mine wrote to me regarding this matter. He writes:
Why only the family entertainment of moving pictures? This includes the poorer classes, children and old folks. What about high-priced hockey, baseball, horse racing? Then again opera, "evening-dress" dramatics, festivals? Community bridge affairs, bingo games, circuses, etc.?
Finally, and I hope this is reached by the minister's taxation proposals:
The pernicious small travelling tent shows, with gambling?
Such as you get at the ordinary fairs in this country. Every year in the maritime provinces there comes a troupe or troupes of people from New England who spend nothing here and who take away immense sums, relatively, from our people. I would clamp the tax right on them.

Would the minister give
thought in this tax to an amusement centre which is wholly municipally owned? Let me cite the case of a city in my district which has issued bonds to the amount of $250,000 for the purpose of establishing a municipal centre. When times were better, it got by. Unfortunately, to-day the city is having to make up the interest. That is a case in which the taxpayers as a whole are taxed further. Unfortunately, conditions there were not so bright as they are in the picture business in this community of Ottawa. In fact, there were two picture houses in that city, and one of
[Mr. Coldwell.l
them had to close for lack of business. I must emphasize that it is a community with more than ordinary patriotic and ambitious spirit because, while it has only about 7,000 people, it has contributed more than a million dollars towards the war loans and war services, and it has given of its men in perhaps a larger percentage than any other community. To place a further burden of taxation, not on excess profits, but on a deficit for each year, makes their burden extremely difficult.
Shall section 13 carry?

There are a large number of sections included in section 13. I wish to take just a moment to talk about the operations under the new sections 127 and 129. Under the former, a person authorized by the minister may examine records, books, accounts and vouchers which shall be open to the inspection of officers authorized by the minister, and if it appears to such person that there has been a violation of the provisions, he may without any warrant or legal authority "seize, take away and retain and hold the said records, books, accounts and vouchers until they are produced in any court proceedings." That is a drastic power to give to anybody who is only an auditor. I suggest that at least there should be some written authority from the minister to the man acting under those circumstances. I do not know what the practice is with regard to excise, but this looks to me like a Hitler method in connection with taxes.
Then, under section 129:
If any person liable to maintain records and books of account for the purposes of this part, has, in the opinion of the minister, failed to maintain adequate records and books of account, the minister may assess the tax payable by such person under this part, and the taxes so assessed shall be deemed to be due and payable forthwith.
Who is to judge whether the records are adequate? That is a drastic power to give to the minister without any right of appeal, or even a hearing. If the man comes along and says that my records are not adequate, he is to be constituted to be the judge, I suppose, under this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Then the minister, without hearing the other side, may assess the tax; the tax shall be forthwith due and payable, and the other fellow is not permitted to say a word about it. The tax is assessed without a hearing and with no right of appeal. I object to it on principle. I am not going to labour the point.

Special War Revenue Act
Is section 13 carried? Carried.
Well, there is no defence? The minister is just going to have the section carried.

Section agreed to.
On section 14-Automobiles.

A portion of this section deals with automobiles. What is the present position with regard to the control of manufacture and importation of automobiles? I raise that question because there seems to be some doubt whether the restrictions as they stand are exactly fair and equitable.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is, I think, asking about the War Exchange Conservation Act.
There is also involved the control of Canadian-produced cars by the controller of motor vehicles.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps it is relevant. I am doubtful. The only ground for arguing that the matter can be brought up here is that these taxes are imposed as part of the control of automobiles. In the War Exchange Conservation Act, which was passed, if I remember correctly, on December 2, the import of automobiles was prohibited and heavy taxes were placed on domestic automobiles. It was found, of course, that dealers of imported automobiles would be out of business so far as the sale of imported automobiles was concerned, although in most instances they had garages and businesses connected with the actual selling of automobiles, which enabled them to go on. Therefore the matter was reconsidered, and it was decided to allow a small importation, upon a quota basis.
Twenty per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For the first three months of 1941, 20 per cent of the number of automobiles imported during the first three months of 1940 were permitted. At the same time a motor vehicle controller was appointed; and since it was not desired that manufacturers of automobiles in this country should be enabled to take advantage of this prohibition of importations to increase their sales, merely taking up the slack created by the prohibition, statistics were obtained and conferences held, and the Canadian manufacturers were placed on quotas. What those quotas are I do not know.
Eighty per cent, I think.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Roughly, it is 80 per cent of the previous year. There are many refinements of those figure*
Does that include 80 per cent of the cars they were producing for export in 1940?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think so. That was for domestic consumption, if I remember correctly.
I believe that is the story in its main outlines. There is one question about the cars which might be assembled in Canada if assembly were permitted, if it was decided to put the assembly of cars on the same basis as imported cars.
It is impossible for these firms to set up plants in Canada now, is it not? Was there not some prohibition?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that is so. Either that, or they get no advantage by doing so; if they do, they are deemed to be importers so far as the quota is concerned. It is either one or the other.	[DOT]

For all practical purposes it is prevented. I suggest to the minister that the size of the quota be reconsidered to determine whether it is fair in all respects. There are many people in this country who are suffering as a result of it. They are, I think, mostly retail dealers, and some of them are in a very, very difficult position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I realize that.

Does the minister hold out hope of any relief for them, because what has been said is too true? Firms with substantial investments in the shape of warehouses, showrooms and service garages are finding the going very difficult; some of them will have to go under. The minister knows of one case which he was good enough to hear at my request. I do not suggest that that gentleman will go under, but he is going behind, It is a great hardship, and I do not know what the answer is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

On the one hand, we must conserve the exchange position; yet, if we do, we shall work grave injustice upon some of our best citizens. It is a, problem with which the minister has to deal.
I have not any solution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the hon, gentleman is very fair about it. Hon. members have no idea of the number of representations which have been made to the government, and made to myself as Minister of Finance, since the passing of that War Exchange Conservation Act. There were representations from young and middle-aged men who had gone into the newsstand business and were relying on United
Special War Revenue Act

States periodicals for a good part of their income. It is all right for members to rise in their places and say that we should shutout the "pulps," and it is probably the right thing to do. As a matter of fact, it is what we are doing with many of the "pulps." But it infringes upon the security and the welfare of people who are engaged in importing and vending these things.
The same applies to dealers in imported automobiles. It might perhaps be said that they knew, when the war came on, it might be necessary for them to adjust themselves and they should have done so. They should have adjusted themselves to the change that was coming, and some did. Some had it in mind and got adjusted and others did not.
Numerous industries, small for the most part, underwent the same experience. The Canadian Importers' association have been making representations continually. I do not know how vigorous or strict the house or the country would like the response to be, but I have taken the view that this was a desperately serious situation and that we had to take such action as we proposed. Undoubtedly, if we wanted to do the popular and easy thing, we would let these dealers bring in their cars, the young men in the newsstand business bring in their "pulps" and the members of the Canadian Importers' association bring in their imports. There are hundreds of articles the importation of which is prohibited, and that has broken right into the living of a great many importers. If we could coast along in a humane and merciful way for the time being we could relax these restrictions and get back to normal, but I do not think we can do that. We have to go along the course we are following.
There may be some adjustments from time to time as in the case of motor cars. The purpose of that quota was not to enable dealers to continue in business on a profitable basis as dealers in motor cars. The quota was not high enough. The purpose was to prevent their cars from disappearing, the names of their cars from being lost to the public, so that they might maintain a connection, keep [DOT] the names of their cars, and sell the odd one during this temporary period. That is not enough to make a living on except where they have garages and other means of income.

There is a possible solution, but I do not know whether we should discuss it. The effect of the restrictions has been practically to give to the big three the whole Canadian market. It is true enough, the quota came on afterwards and to a degree cut in on that. But the big three have their agents in particular communities.

If an arrangement could be made by the motor vehicle controller with any reputable dealer who had credit or cash, he could go to one of the big three and purchase on terms similar to or equally advantageous with those of recognized agents; he would have a chance to sell through the domestic production, and in that way these people might be kept in business. That, I admit, is something of state socialism, but it is the only solution that has entered my head with regard to this problem. But they will not look at the man who has been frozen out. Take General Motors or any of these big corporations. They have good dealers in their communities and can pick and choose because they have the cars the public want; yet here is another man who may have equally good credit facilities, who has been selling the Packard or the Studebaker. He is put out of business. If some arrangement could be made by the motor vehicle controller so as to have this business spread round, that might be a solution. I do not urge it; I merely suggest it.

The average soft drink
is five cents a bottle. How can 25 per cent be applied to a five-cent bottle and the retail price be suitably arranged?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The tax is on the manufacturer, and if he has to raise the retail price as a result of the tax, I suppose he does so.

Section agreed to.
On section 15-Sugar.

I have
something to say on this section. After what I heard in this house in 1933 from certain hon. gentlemen opposite, many of whom are absent, I never thought I would live to see the day when the Liberal party would impose an additional tax on sugar. The tax on sugar in 1933 was put on by the Bennett administration not because they wanted to put it on; it was put on to raise and support the revenues of the country at a time of dire economic necessity when, as a result of the stress of a world-wide economic depression, our revenues were visibly falling. Sugar was singled out because it was an article of universal consumption which the common people and the rich people alike use, and it was thought it would bring in an estimated revenue of $20,000,000. There was a war on then.
Isn't there now?

Yes. What was the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite? That was a world-wide economic war. I wonder whether the Minister of National Defence was through it? He was not in the

Special War Revenue Act
house at the time, but we went through it. How much assistance did we get from hon. gentlemen opposite?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend means the
Minister of National Revenue.

Yes, the
Minister of National Revenue. How much assistance did we get?
Nothing but abuse.

Absolutely nothing but abuse. I have here excerpts of some remarks made, perhaps from this very seat, by certain hon. gentlemen opposite. They condemned us in no uncertain terms for putting a tax on the poor, common people of the country, about whom they were so much concerned, and in the election of 1935 they pledged their party to the repeal of the sugar tax. But they never did it. We reduced the tax to a cent a pound before 1935, but these gentlemen went up and down the country to the housewives and condemned the Bennett government for the sugar tax, which was imposed at a time of great national distress. But they did not keep their word; the tax of one cent a pound on sugar remained.
They never do.

I will not say they never do; but they seldom do. They do not when it does not suit their convenience. Among the most vociferous at that time was the present Minister of National Defence who was then financial critic of the opposition. What did he say? He was as bitter and as picayune as I ever heard him in my life, and he could be picayune when he wanted to. As reported at page 3372 of Hansard for March 24, 1933, he said:
Let us consider for a moment the other taxes. There is to be a tax of two cents per pound on sugar, and I understand that molasses is taken from the exempted list under the sales tax. We are told that $20,000,000 is expected to be raised from the tax on sugar.
This is the appeal against the tax.
That amounts to $2 per head for every man, woman and child in this dominion and I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this tax, bearing as it does upon a necessity of life that always has been regarded as an essential, coupled with the removal of molasses from the list of exempted goods under the sales tax, imposes a very great hardship on the poorer people of this dominion.
I pause there. That was the text for the whole band-I was going to say of outlaws- who traduced this party from one end of Canada to the other. My opponent in 1935, a millionaire, made the sugar tax the basis of his attack on me, and I have no doubt that it helped defeat me.

Was he a sugar
millionaire?

No; he
was a man who all his life had farmed the farmers of this country. He is still living; he is still farming. I venture to say that this statement of the present Minister of National Defence was the basis of the most violent attacks ever made on any government; and the present Minister of Finance himself voted against that tax. I know the answer will be that we are at war, and that is true; but I say to hon. members that in 1933 we were also at war, an economic war, which had dire consequences on this country. The statement I have read was made by the financial critic of the Liberal party, and it was the text for the whole gang of wolves who were on our trail all over this country. At that time the Liberal party was not quite so close to the sugar industry as it is to-day; it did not have the backing of certain people that it has to-day. The present Minister of National Defence went on to say:
So far as the sugar industry is concerned, I have no fault to find with my hon. friend. That industry is well protected; in fact it is too well protected-
Well, it is still well protected; that is the only observation I have to make.
[DOT]-but this tax is not going to be paid by the sugar industry. This tax of two cents a pound will be paid by the individual householder who, with sugar at the present price, will have to pay a fifty per cent tax on all the sugar going into his house.
Do you see the insidiousness of that appeal: a fifty per cent tax, and this was at a time when sugar was probably at the lowest point in its history.
And everything else, too.

Yes, I
regret to say that is true; and things were even lower in the United States than in Canada. I remember that after we entered into the Ottawa agreements I motored from Winnipeg to Toronto, passing through the United States. Just outside Hillsboro, North Dakota, we had two punctures, and the farmer came down to see us. He told us that he was a hog raiser, and what do you suppose he was getting for his hogs on the Chicago market in the spring of 1934? He was getting two and a quarter cents a pound, as opposed to eight and a half cents a pound here.

What did the hon. member
for Brant get that year?

I got three and a quarter
cents.

Then you had better go back to your dealer, because you have something more coming to you. Those two statements by the present Minister of National Defence formed the basis for the attack that was made upon us in this house. Then Mr. Howard, who at that time was the member for Sherbrooke and' who now has gone to his reward in another place, proclaimed himself a great friend of the common people and said:
I want to protest in the strongest words I can use against this tax of two cents per pound on granulated white sugar, a commodity which perhaps is in greater demand than most any other product in Canada. At least, it has a wider distribution than any other product I know of. The tax is an enormous one. . . .
Then there was a gentleman here representing the consituency of Lisgar, Mr. Brown by name. Do hon. gentlemen remember him? I am not going to say anything about him or what he said, because I understand that now he has gone to his reward.
No.

No? All right; he is gone out of this house. I thought he was dead, but apparently he [DOT] is only politically dead. He still has a chance for repentance, because he will never come back. As reported at page 4478 of Hansard he said in that budget debate:
The fact is that the tax is a very heavy burden on the people of Canada, and the magnitude of that burden can be to some extent appreciated when I recall the fact I mentioned in the budget debate that about fifty million bushels is the amount of wheat that is consumed by the people of Canada. At fifty cents a bushel that would mean $25,000,000, and I believe the estimated revenue from the sugar tax is $20,000,000, or only $5,000,000 short of the total value of the wheat consumed by the people of Canada. That comparison shows the magnitude of the burden that is imposed upon the consumer by this sugar tax.
I could quote many more statements by that same gentleman. Then there was a member from Hamilton East, Mr. Mitchell, who is not now in this house, but who has received his reward elsewhere. He had this to say:
... it represents a taxation upon every man, woman and child in Canada, and places a further burden upon the 1,300,000 people drawing relief.
Then there was the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly), who I am sorry is not in his seat to-night. He had a great deal to say about that tax. I could go on right through this long list of extracts, but I really have not the heart to detain the committee for that length of time. There was the member for Melville, Mr. Motherwell. What gems he used to get off in this house! I understand that after 1935 his shafts were not always aimed at this party, but were sometimes
[Mr. Wood.l
directed towards his own friends. That may have been a case of sour grapes, I do not know; at all events I must confess to always having had a very warm spot in my heart for the former member for Melville. He certainly was a picturesque figure in this house, and he certainly knew something about agriculture. Of course, I could not expect that he should know as much as the present hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner), his successor in office.

But I
certainly had not, and have not to-day, any antagonistic feeling toward the then member for Melville. He said, as regards the sugar tax:
I do not see how I can allow this to go by without protesting. After hearing-
Just listen to this.
-some of the letters read yesterday on behalf of the women and children of the country-
The poor women and children!-when sugar was down, we shall say, to two cents or four cents a pound, and a tax of two cents was being put on.
-and listening to the protests that came from every quarter on this side of the house, yes, and the silent protest of the rear-guard supporting the government-because I know they entertain such protests-I am wondering whether the minister is not considering the advisability of abandoning this tax. Then there was the member who then represented the constituency of Prince, Prince Edward Island. I shall not say anything about that gentleman, because he has gone to his reward. And I shall skip over the former member for Middlesex West.

Hear, hear.

This tax of two cents on sugar amounts to practically 50 per cent of the value of the article, a very heavy tax indeed-
He took his cue from his colleagues.
-it strikes at everybody, and this is an article of food. I think it is very regrettable, though perhaps in some degree necessary, that we should have taxation on food.
